lead: This unit shows how a fast switch, a diode and an inductor turn one DC voltage into another with little waste. After it you can read any buck, boost, buck-boost, flyback or forward circuit, write its gain formula, sketch its waveforms and pick its inductor, transformer and capacitor.
about: The unit is about changing DC voltage efficiently. Chapter 3.1 gives the chopper idea — one switch, one diode, one duty ratio — and the three ways to control it. Chapter 3.2 compares the linear regulator, which burns the extra voltage as heat, with the switched-mode supply that chops it instead. Chapters 3.3 to 3.5 build the basic cells: buck, boost, buck-boost and Cuk, each with its two switching states, waveform analysis and gain formula. Chapter 3.6 adds a transformer for isolation and voltage ratio in the flyback and forward converters. Chapter 3.7 shows that small magnetics need high switching frequency, high frequency brings switching loss, and resonant soft switching removes that loss. Chapter 3.8 turns every formula into numbers: core, turns, wire, ESR and temperature rise.

chapters.idea: A chopper is a switch that opens and closes quickly between a DC source and its load, so the average load voltage is set by the fraction of each period the switch stays on.
chapters.depth: Draw the basic chopper: source V_s, switch (MOSFET or IGBT with its gate driver), freewheeling diode and load. Define period T = 1/f_s, on-time T_on, off-time T_off and duty ratio D = T_on/T, with D between 0 and 1. Show that for a resistive load with a freewheeling diode the average load voltage is V_o = D·V_s and the average current is D·V_s/R. Cover the three control strategies: constant-frequency pulse-width (time-ratio) control, variable-frequency control, and current-limit control; explain the trade-off between them (fixed-frequency control gives predictable filter design but fixed switching loss; variable frequency keeps the pulse fixed but makes filter design harder). Classify choppers as step-down, step-up, step-down/step-up and Cuk, and name the two conduction modes, continuous (CCM) and discontinuous (DCM), in one line each. Some syllabi say 'DC chopper' or 'buck chopper' where others say 'DC-DC converter'; use both names. Keep the gain derivations for the later chapters.
chapters.example: A DC chopper feeds a 10 Ω resistor from a 200 V DC source. The switching frequency is 1 kHz and the on-time is 0.4 ms. (a) Find the duty ratio, average output voltage, average output current and output power. (b) The frequency is now raised to 2 kHz with the same 0.4 ms on-time; find D, V_o and the power. Answer: T = 1 ms, D = 0.4 ms / 1 ms = 0.4, V_o = 0.4 × 200 V = 80 V, I_o = 80 V / 10 Ω = 8 A, P_o = 640 W. At 2 kHz, T = 0.5 ms, D = 0.4 / 0.5 = 0.8, V_o = 160 V, I_o = 16 A, P_o = 2560 W — the same on-time gives double the voltage because the period shrank.
chapters.trap: D is T_on/T, never T_off/T. Also V_o = D·V_s is the average voltage only because the freewheeling diode holds the load current during the off-time; without it a resistive load simply follows the switch and the average is the same but the current is pulsed.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for the switch and diode, their on-state drops and gate drive; Unit 2 for the idea of an average voltage from a switched source.
chapters.leave: Device switching times, snubbers and junction temperature to Unit 1; inverter switching to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A linear regulator controls output voltage by dropping the excess voltage across a pass transistor as heat, while a switched-mode power supply chops and filters instead, reaching 70-95 % efficiency at the cost of ripple and EMI.
chapters.depth: Linear regulator: series pass transistor (or Darlington) working in its active region, error amplifier comparing a fraction of V_o with a zener or bandgap reference, dropout voltage, and shutdown below it. Give efficiency η = V_o/V_in and dissipation P_d = (V_in − V_o)·I_o on the pass device, and say that this heat sets the heat-sink size from Unit 1. Mention shunt regulators and low-dropout (LDO) types in one line. Switched-mode supply: block chain of rectifier and filter, high-frequency switch, transformer or inductor, output rectifier, L-C filter and PWM controller with isolated feedback (optocoupler or auxiliary winding). Steady-state loss is conduction loss plus switching loss, so efficiency is high and the magnetics shrink as frequency rises. Discuss low-power high-frequency adapters used for phone chargers, laptop bricks and LED drivers: typical switching frequency tens of kHz to a few hundred kHz, but cost is EMI, output ripple and control complexity. Compare the two side by side in a table.

figure.title: Two ways to drop 12 V to 5 V

chapters.example: A 5 V linear regulator takes 1 A from a 12 V input. (a) Find the pass-transistor dissipation and the efficiency. (b) A switched-mode supply of 85 % efficiency does the same job; find its input power and its loss. Answer: P_d = (12 − 5) V × 1 A = 7 W; η = 5/12 = 41.7 %. For the SMPS, P_o = 5 V × 1 A = 5 W, P_in = 5/0.85 = 5.88 W, loss = 0.88 W — about eight times less heat for the same output.
chapters.trap: Linear-regulator loss is (V_in − V_o)·I_o, not V_in·I_o. SMPS efficiency is P_o/P_in; V_o/V_in is meaningless for a switcher, which can even step up.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for the MOSFET switch and its drive, Unit 2 for the rectifier and capacitor filter at the input.
chapters.leave: Heat-sink sizing formulas to Unit 1; power factor correction of the input rectifier to Unit 2; UPS systems to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The buck converter puts the switch-diode pair before an L-C filter, so the inductor averages the chopped voltage down: V_o = D·V_s in continuous conduction.
chapters.depth: Draw the circuit: V_s, switch S, freewheeling (catch) diode, inductor L, capacitor C, load R. Analyse the two states. ON: v_L = V_s − V_o, current rises. OFF: the diode conducts, v_L = −V_o, current falls. Apply volt-second balance over one period, D(V_s − V_o) = (1 − D)V_o, to get D = V_o/V_s and V_o < V_s. Derive the current ripple ΔI_L = (V_s − V_o)·D·T/L = V_o(1 − D)/(f_s·L), give peak and minimum current I_o ± ΔI_L/2, and the CCM boundary L_min = (1 − D)V_o/(2 f_s I_o). Derive output ripple ΔV_o = ΔI_L/(8 f_s C). Draw the gate pulse, inductor current, diode and switch currents. Mention the synchronous buck, where a second MOSFET replaces the diode for low-voltage high-current loads, and the effect of the diode drop (V_o = D·V_s − V_D(1 − D) roughly). Some syllabi call this the 'buck chopper' or 'step-down chopper'. Keep DCM to one line: gain rises above D·V_s at light load.
chapters.example: A buck converter has V_s = 50 V, D = 0.4, f_s = 100 kHz, L = 100 µH, C = 220 µF and a 5 Ω load. Find V_o, the inductor ripple, the peak and minimum inductor current, the output ripple, and the inductance at the CCM boundary. Answer: V_o = 0.4 × 50 = 20 V; I_o = 20/5 = 4 A; T = 10 µs and T_on = 4 µs; ΔI_L = (50 − 20) × 4 µs / 100 µH = 1.2 A, so i_L swings between 3.4 A and 4.6 A and stays continuous. Output ripple ΔV_o = 1.2 A / (8 × 100 kHz × 220 µF) = 6.8 mV. Boundary L = (1 − 0.4) × 20 V / (2 × 100 kHz × 4 A) = 15 µH, so 100 µH is safely in CCM.
chapters.trap: V_o = D·V_s is a CCM result; in DCM the output floats upward toward V_s as the load lightens. Also use v_L = V_s − V_o during the on-time — forgetting the output term is the commonest slip.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 for duty ratio and CCM, Chapter 3.2 for where the filter sits in an SMPS; Unit 2 for capacitor filtering.
chapters.leave: Device selection and switching loss to Unit 1; closed-loop compensator design is not in most syllabi.

chapters.idea: The boost converter charges an inductor from the source with the switch on, then puts that inductor in series with the source through a diode, so the output is always higher than the input: V_o = V_s/(1 − D).
chapters.depth: Draw the circuit: V_s, inductor L, switch S to the return rail, diode D to the output capacitor C and load. Analyse the two states: ON, v_L = V_s, current rises by V_s·D·T/L; OFF, v_L = V_s − V_o (negative), current falls by (V_o − V_s)(1 − D)T/L. Volt-second balance gives V_o = V_s/(1 − D), and D = 1 − V_s/V_o. Stress that D must stay below about 0.9 in practice because the gain grows without limit and losses take over. Give ripple ΔI_L = V_s·D/(f_s·L), the average inductor current I_L = I_o/(1 − D), the CCM boundary L_min = V_s·D·T/(2 I_L) and the extra output ripple ΔV_o = I_o·D/(f_s·C) because the capacitor alone feeds the load during the on-time. Draw the waveforms. Explain why the input current is smooth (the inductor is in series with the source) and why the output current is pulsed, and note the right-half-plane zero that makes the loop slower than a buck's. Note the alternative name 'step-up chopper' and the use of this cell in power-factor-correction front ends and battery-to-rail boosters.
chapters.example: A boost converter runs from 24 V with D = 0.6, f_s = 50 kHz, L = 300 µH, C = 470 µF and a 100 Ω load. Find V_o, I_o, the average and ripple inductor current, and the output ripple. Answer: T = 20 µs; V_o = 24/(1 − 0.6) = 60 V; I_o = 60/100 = 0.6 A; I_L = 0.6/0.4 = 1.5 A; ΔI_L = 24 × 0.6 × 20 µs / 300 µH = 0.96 A, so i_L moves between 1.02 A and 1.98 A and stays continuous. Output ripple ΔV_o = 0.6 A × 0.6 / (50 kHz × 470 µF) = 15.3 mV.
chapters.trap: The boost switch carries the full inductor current, not the load current, and the diode conducts only during the off-time. Writing V_o = V_s·D or forgetting the (1 − D) in the current transfer are the usual errors.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.3 for volt-second balance and ripple formulas; Unit 1 for the switch rating.
chapters.leave: PFC boost front ends to Unit 2; battery-to-bus boosting in solar and UPS systems to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The buck-boost converter uses the same inductor first to store and then to deliver energy with reversed output polarity, giving V_o = −V_s·D/(1 − D); the Cuk converter reaches the same gain with a capacitor in the middle and smooth currents at both ports.
chapters.depth: Buck-boost: draw V_s, switch, inductor, diode and output capacitor. ON: the inductor takes V_s, the diode is off and the capacitor feeds the load. OFF: the inductor current flows through the diode into the output, so v_L = V_o (which is negative). Volt-second balance D·V_s + (1 − D)·V_o = 0 gives V_o = −V_s·D/(1 − D); the magnitude can be below or above V_s, hence 'step-down/step-up' or 'inverting regulator'. Give the switch and diode voltage stress V_s + |V_o|, the average inductor current I_L = I_o/(1 − D), and say the input current is pulsed, which needs a good input capacitor. Cuk: draw L1, switch, coupling capacitor C1, diode, L2 and the output. Show that the average voltage across C1 is V_s + |V_o| and the gain is again −D/(1 − D), but now both input and output currents are continuous, which lowers ripple; the price is two inductors and a capacitor that carries a large AC current. Mention SEPIC and Zeta as relatives in one line.
chapters.example: A buck-boost converter takes 12 V and must deliver 18 V into a 10 Ω load at 100 kHz. Find the duty ratio, the output current, the inductor current and the voltage stress on the switch. Answer: gain magnitude 18/12 = 1.5 = D/(1 − D), so D = 0.6; I_o = 18/10 = 1.8 A; I_L = I_o/(1 − D) = 1.8/0.4 = 4.5 A; voltage stress = V_s + |V_o| = 12 + 18 = 30 V, and the output is −18 V with respect to the common rail. A Cuk converter with the same D and turns-free components gives the same −18 V but with continuous input current.
chapters.trap: Sign and ratio: the output is inverted and the gain is D/(1 − D), not (1 − D)/D; swapping them gives a number that looks plausible at D = 0.5 where both equal 1.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.3 and 3.4 for the on/off state analysis and volt-second balance.
chapters.leave: SEPIC, Zeta and isolated versions to Chapter 3.6; control loop design is outside most syllabi.

chapters.idea: An isolated converter puts a transformer between the switch and the load: the flyback stores energy in the transformer during the on-time and delivers it during the off-time, while the forward converter delivers energy during the on-time and needs a way to reset the core.
chapters.depth: Say why isolation is wanted: safety, a large step-up or step-down ratio, and several outputs. Flyback: the transformer is really a coupled inductor with an air gap; the primary inductance is the energy-storing element. ON: primary current ramps, secondary diode is reverse biased. OFF: the stored energy transfers, the secondary diode conducts. In CCM with n = N1/N2, V_o = V_s·D/((1 − D)·n). Give the switch stress V_s + n·V_o plus the leakage-inductance spike, and the RCD clamp or snubber that absorbs it. Forward: primary and secondary conduct together through the transformer and an output inductor, so V_o = V_s·D·(N2/N1); the output stage looks like a buck. The core must be reset every cycle, by a third reset winding (D must stay below 0.5 when it has the same turns as the primary) or by an active clamp; otherwise the core walks into saturation. Compare: flyback is simple and cheap for low power (phone chargers, standby supplies), forward suits medium power, and both trade a leakage spike and a duty limit against isolation.
chapters.example: A flyback converter runs from 48 V DC at 100 kHz with a transformer of 40 primary turns and 20 secondary turns, so n = N1/N2 = 2. (a) Find V_o at D = 0.4. (b) Find the duty ratio needed for 12 V output. (c) Find the switch voltage stress, ignoring the leakage spike. Answer: (a) V_o = 48 × 0.4 / (0.6 × 2) = 16 V. (b) 12 = 48 × D / (2(1 − D)) gives 24(1 − D) = 48D, so D = 24/72 = 0.333. (c) Stress = V_s + n·V_o = 48 + 2 × 12 = 72 V at 12 V output (80 V at 16 V output), so a 150 V device is a sensible choice.
chapters.trap: The flyback turns ratio sits in the denominator of the CCM gain because the switch voltage — not the output — is applied to the primary while energy is stored; using V_o = V_s·D·(N2/N1) on a flyback is wrong. Also D must be limited on a forward converter, or the core saturates.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.3 and 3.5 for buck-type output stages and duty ratio; Unit 1 for device voltage ratings and snubbers.
chapters.leave: Transformer core loss and window design to Chapter 3.8; full-bridge isolated supplies are outside most syllabi.

chapters.idea: Small magnetics need a high switching frequency, high frequency makes the switch lose power during every voltage-current overlap, and resonant soft switching removes that overlap by forcing the voltage or the current to zero before the switch changes state.
chapters.depth: Start from the hard-switching loss with a linear overlap: P_sw = ½·V·I·(t_r + t_f)·f_s, plus the diode's reverse-recovery loss and the energy dumped from the device capacitance. Add the conduction loss I²·R_on and show that the total has a minimum at some frequency, which is why plain PWM tops out. Then define soft switching: zero-voltage switching (ZVS) turns the device on only after its voltage has fallen to zero, zero-current switching (ZCS) turns it off only after its current has fallen to zero. Show the resonant switch idea: an inductor L_r and capacitor C_r form a tank with f_0 = 1/(2π√(L_r·C_r)) and the switch is timed to the tank's zero crossings, so the device transition happens at zero. Classify briefly: load-resonant series and parallel converters, resonant switch (quasi-resonant) converters, and the LLC circuit common in adapters. Say that the gain of a resonant converter is set by switching frequency rather than duty ratio, that the regulation range is narrower, and that only a few universities derive the resonant gain curves — usually the exam only asks for the loss comparison and the ZVS/ZCS definitions.
chapters.example: A MOSFET switches 200 V and 5 A at 100 kHz with rise and fall times of 100 ns each, and the voltage and current overlap fully during each transition. Its on-resistance is 0.1 Ω. (a) Find the switching loss. (b) Find the conduction loss. (c) Find the loss after ZVS removes the turn-on overlap. Answer: (a) P_sw = ½ × 200 V × 5 A × (100 + 100) ns × 100 kHz = 500 × 200e-9 × 1e5 = 10 W. (b) P_cond = 5² × 0.1 = 2.5 W. (c) Only the turn-off overlap remains, about 5 W, so total loss falls from 12.5 W to 7.5 W — and both transitions can be softened in a full resonant design.
chapters.trap: The ½ in the overlap formula assumes triangular voltage and current; using V·I·t·f without it doubles the answer. And ZVS removes the turn-on loss, not the conduction loss — the device still carries current.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for switching loss, output capacitance and heat sinks; Chapters 3.3 to 3.5 for the PWM cells the resonant tank replaces.
chapters.leave: Resonant inverter control and grid-tied operation to Unit 4; detailed thermal calculation to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Design means turning the ripple formulas into a core, a number of turns, an air gap, a wire gauge and a capacitor ESR that keep flux, current density and temperature inside their limits.
chapters.depth: Inductor: from the converter chapter take L, the average current, the ripple and therefore the peak current I_pk = I_avg + ΔI_L/2. Choose a core with effective area A_e and a peak flux density B_max (about 0.3 T for ferrite), then N = L·I_pk/(B_max·A_e); check B with the chosen N. Energy in a gapped core is stored mostly in the air gap, so gap length and saturation current are designed together. Pick wire from a current density of 2 to 4 A/mm² and remember skin depth δ = √(ρ/(π·f·µ)) — at 100 kHz in copper it is a fraction of a millimetre, so use several strands or litz wire. Add copper loss I²R and core loss, and check the temperature rise. Transformer: turns ratio from the gain formula, then window area must hold both windings, and core loss rises with frequency and flux swing. Capacitor: capacitance from the ripple formula, but also check ESR, because ΔV_o is often set by ESR × ΔI_L rather than by C, plus the RMS ripple-current rating and derating of electrolytics; ceramic capacitors have low ESR and suit high frequency. Close with a thermal check: total loss times thermal resistance gives the temperature rise.
chapters.example: Design the inductor for the buck converter of Chapter 3.3: V_s = 50 V, V_o = 20 V, I_o = 4 A, f_s = 100 kHz, L = 100 µH, ripple 1.2 A. The core has A_e = 1.0 cm² = 1.0e-4 m² and B_max = 0.3 T. (a) Find the peak current. (b) Find the number of turns. (c) Find the copper area for J = 4 A/mm². Answer: (a) I_pk = 4 + 0.6 = 4.6 A. (b) N = (100e-6 × 4.6) / (0.3 × 1.0e-4) = 4.6e-4 / 3.0e-5 = 15.3, so use 16 turns; then B = 4.6e-4 / (16 × 1.0e-4) = 0.29 T, below the limit. (c) Area = 4 A / 4 A/mm² = 1 mm², a wire of about 1.1 mm diameter — or several thinner strands to beat skin effect.
chapters.trap: Sizing the core on the average current instead of the peak lets it saturate on every cycle, and the inductance collapses. Also the output ripple is often ESR-driven, so choosing C from ΔI/(8fC) alone gives a capacitor that misses the specification.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.3 to 3.6 for the L, C and ripple values, Chapter 3.7 for the high-frequency loss and skin effect; Unit 1 for thermal resistance and heat sinks.
chapters.leave: Device junction temperature and heat-sink selection to Unit 1; EMI filter design is outside most syllabi.
